steps.body: Spread five buttons far apart and the group LOOKS bigger — but looking bigger and being more are different. The count ends at five.
steps.narration: Spread five buttons far apart and the group LOOKS bigger — but looking bigger and being more are different. The count ends at five.

widget.prompt: The 5 buttons were spread far apart. Count them again and show the answer.

commonCounts.feedback: The empty space holds no buttons; spreading cannot add one.
That reads the gaps as swallowing buttons — but empty space holds nothing, and touching each button still ends the count at 5.

widget.missFeedback: Ignore the spacing: touch each button once and the count ends where it always did.
widget.successFeedback: Five, exactly as before — the gaps grew, the group did not.

predict.prompt: 5 buttons are spread far apart. More buttons now?
predict.reveal: Spreading changes where the buttons sit, not how many there are.

cml.actionGoal: Pair each object with exactly one number and trust the last number said for kch conservation.
invariants: A count pairs objects with number words one to one, and its last word names the whole group — which is why order, spacing, and arrangement can change without changing the answer for kch conservation.
misconceptions: Skipping or double-counting an object, recounting when nothing changed, or believing a spread-out group holds more.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: If one more object joined the group, what would the last counting word become?

widget.prompt: 5 buttons are spread far apart. Are there more buttons now?

options.label: No — spreading changes the space, not the count
options.feedback: Correct — the buttons look bigger as a group, but each one still gets one number and the count ends at 5.

options.label: Yes — they take up more room
options.feedback: Room is not amount; the same 5 buttons are simply farther apart.

options.label: Fewer — the gaps swallow some
options.feedback: Gaps hold no buttons; all 5 are still there to be counted.

options.label: You must weigh them to know
options.feedback: Counting answers how many; spreading them out changes nothing it measures.

widget.prompt: Compare 9 and 9. Which statement is true?

options.label: They are equal
options.feedback: Correct — the same numeral names the same amount every time, so the two match exactly.

options.label: The first number is greater
options.feedback: Both numbers are 9, so neither one is greater than the other.

options.label: 9 is less than 9
options.feedback: A number cannot be less than itself; the two values are equal.

options.label: You cannot tell
options.feedback: You can tell at a glance — the numerals are identical, so the amounts are too.

widget.prompt: Start at 3. Hop forward 4 times by 1. Where do you land?

commonLandings.feedback: 6 stops one complete hop too soon. Continue the final 1-unit hop to reach 7.
8 goes one complete hop too far. Count just 4 hops from 3 to land on 7.

widget.missFeedback: Start at 3 and count on 4: you land on 7.
widget.successFeedback: 3 and 4 more is 7 — each hop says the next counting number.
widget.lowFeedback: Short of the landing — count all 4 hops, one number per hop, to reach 7.
widget.highFeedback: Past the landing — the count stops after exactly 4 hops, on 7.

options.feedback: Correct — the last number said, 4, tells how many blocks there are in all.
The count stops at 4; saying one more number would count a block that is not there.
That stops one number early — every block gets exactly one number, ending at 4.
